account: On 21 February 2023 Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud's Constitution Bench heard the Maharashtra political crisis matter in Court Room 1. It used AI live transcription supplied by TERES, with screens facing the lawyers showing the text. The Chief Justice called it an experiment. He said that transcripts would go to lawyers for verification and then onto the Supreme Court website (LiveLaw, 21 February 2023). The Supreme Court Observer reported on 18 May 2023 that 25 Constitution Bench hearings had been held across four cases. Only nine transcripts had been published: six for the marriage-equality case, three for the Maharashtra case and none for the other two. None was published in March 2023. NDTV reported on 8 December 2023 a written reply in the Lok Sabha by Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal. He said that AI transcription had been deployed for Constitution Bench matters since February. He said that transcripts in almost ten main matters had been generated and published on the court's website. The use was on a trial basis. The Supreme Court Observer reported on 20 February 2024 that transcripts were by then regularly published on the court website within days of a Constitution Bench hearing. It also reported that Justice Sanjiv Khanna reproduced part of a hearing transcript in the Electoral Bonds judgment of 15 February 2024. A Press Information Bureau feature of 11 February 2026 states that the system is being extended to regular hearing days. It says that the extension follows successful use in Constitution Bench proceedings.

ai_role.statement: The AI produced the live draft. Lawyers proofread before publication and, per the Chief Justice, people oversee overlapping speech. The published-transcript rate (36% of hearings by May 2023) shows the benefit depended as much on human vetting as on the recognizer.

fields.account: On 21 February 2023 Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud's Constitution Bench heard the Maharashtra political crisis matter in Court Room 1. It used AI live transcription supplied by TERES, with screens facing the lawyers showing the text. The Chief Justice called it an experiment. He said that transcripts would go to lawyers for verification and then onto the Supreme Court website (LiveLaw, 21 February 2023). The Supreme Court Observer reported on 18 May 2023 that 25 Constitution Bench hearings had been held across four cases. Only nine transcripts had been published: six for the marriage-equality case, three for the Maharashtra case and none for the other two. None was published in March 2023. NDTV reported on 8 December 2023 a written reply in the Lok Sabha by Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal. He said that AI transcription had been deployed for Constitution Bench matters since February. He said that transcripts in almost ten main matters had been generated and published on the court's website. The use was on a trial basis. The Supreme Court Observer reported on 20 February 2024 that transcripts were by then regularly published on the court website within days of a Constitution Bench hearing. It also reported that Justice Sanjiv Khanna reproduced part of a hearing transcript in the Electoral Bonds judgment of 15 February 2024. A Press Information Bureau feature of 11 February 2026 states that the system is being extended to regular hearing days. It says that the extension follows successful use in Constitution Bench proceedings.
fields.summary: From 21 February 2023 the Supreme Court of India transcribed Constitution Bench hearings live with an AI service from TERES, and by February 2024 transcripts appeared on its website within days.

purpose: The transcription was introduced to give judges, lawyers and law colleges a record of arguments and to make the court a court of record. Published transcripts serve that purpose.

ratings.reason: The court gained lawyer-verified transcripts of Constitution Bench hearings on a trial basis. It had published them for 9 of 25 hearings by May 2023 and for almost ten main matters by December 2023, and by February 2024 it published them regularly within days of a hearing.

Transcripts were published on the court's website for public and academic use, for only a minority of hearings in the first months. By February 2024 they appeared regularly within days of a hearing, and a judge reproduced part of one in the Electoral Bonds judgment.
